title: Saudi Strikes Yemen’s Houthis, Intercepts Missiles & Drones Amid Rising Middle East Tensions
body:
The Saudi‑led coalition announced a fresh wave of air strikes against Houthi‑controlled facilities in Yemen on Friday, saying the attacks hit key nodes used to smuggle and move weapons through the Red Sea port of Hodeidah and the rebel‑held capital of Sanaa. The operation, which also involved the interception of several missiles and unmanned aerial systems launched from Houthi positions, marks the most intense round of combat in the war’s northern theater in months and underscores the coalition’s intent to cripple the insurgents’ logistics chain ahead of a planned diplomatic push on the conflict’s future.

According to the coalition’s military spokesman, aircraft and naval assets targeted warehouses, depots and transport routes that the Houthis rely on to funnel arms from Iran and other external supporters into the battlefield. “We have disrupted the enemy’s ability to move weapons across the country,” the spokesman said, adding that the strikes were carried out in compliance with international law and with minimal risk to civilian infrastructure. The coalition also reported that its air defenses successfully shot down three ballistic missiles and intercepted two drones that were launched toward Saudi territory from Houthi‑controlled areas, preventing potential damage to critical oil facilities in the kingdom.

The Houthi movement, which seized control of large swaths of northern Yemen in 2014 and has been backed by Tehran, responded with a barrage of rockets aimed at Saudi border towns and a renewed barrage of missile launches toward the Red Sea. While the coalition claimed to have neutralized most of the incoming projectiles, Houthi officials warned that the attacks would only intensify, describing the strikes as “aggression against the Yemeni people” and vowing to continue their “resistance” against what they call an “imperialist coalition.” The exchange of fire has raised concerns among humanitarian agencies that the renewed fighting could further impede aid deliveries through Hodeidah, a vital lifeline for millions of Yemenis already facing famine and disease.

Analysts note that the timing of the operation aligns with a broader regional recalibration. In recent weeks, Saudi Arabia has been navigating a delicate diplomatic landscape, balancing its hardline stance against the Houthis with ongoing negotiations aimed at normalising relations with Iran and securing a cease‑fire framework for Yemen. The intensified military pressure may be intended to strengthen Saudi Arabia’s bargaining position ahead of any talks, signaling that the kingdom will not tolerate any perceived escalation of Iranian influence on its southern border. Moreover, the strikes come as the United Nations continues to push for a comprehensive peace process, with Secretary‑General António Guterres warning that the conflict could spiral into a broader regional conflagration if external powers keep fueling the war.

The humanitarian fallout remains stark. Hodeidah, which handles roughly 70 percent of Yemen’s humanitarian imports, has already seen its port facilities damaged in previous clashes. Any further disruption could exacerbate the already dire food security situation, where the United Nations estimates that more than 20 million Yemenis are on the brink of famine. Aid agencies have called for an immediate cease‑fire and the establishment of protected corridors to ensure the safe passage of relief supplies. The coalition’s claim of “minimal civilian impact” will likely be scrutinised by independent monitors, who have repeatedly documented collateral damage from air strikes in densely populated areas.

Looking ahead, the next few weeks will be critical in determining whether the heightened military campaign will translate into tangible diplomatic gains or simply deepen the cycle of retaliation. If the coalition can indeed cripple the Houthis’ supply lines without causing a humanitarian catastrophe, it may force the insurgents back to the negotiating table under more favorable terms for Saudi Arabia and its allies. Conversely, a protracted escalation could draw in additional regional actors, complicate peace efforts, and further imperil the civilian population. International observers will be watching closely as both sides navigate the fine line between military objectives and the urgent need for a sustainable resolution to Yemen’s protracted war.
